title: Drafting and editing without losing your meaning

sections.skill: Use AI for drafts and edits while keeping your meaning and voice

questions.prompt: What is a risk of having a tool edit your writing?

choices.text: It cannot change any words at all
It will always make your writing sound more like you than before
It can change your meaning or add facts
It makes writing impossible to read

questions.correct_answer: It can change your meaning or add facts
questions.intro: AI tools can help you DRAFT (write a first version) and EDIT (improve clarity, grammar, tone or length). The risk is that the result stops being YOURS: a tool may change your meaning, add facts you did not provide, drop important details, or replace your voice with generic phrases. Good habits: give your own notes or draft as the starting point, say what must not change ("keep my examples and my opinion"), ask for specific edits ("shorten to 150 words" or "fix grammar only"), and reread the result to make sure every sentence is something you mean and can stand behind.
questions.feedback: Edits can drift from your meaning.

questions.prompt: What does "Just a trim, keep the length" do?

choices.text: Asks for a completely new style that the barber picks freely
Asks for a shave
Asks the barber to stop cutting
States what to change and what to keep

questions.correct_answer: States what to change and what to keep
questions.intro: When you get a haircut, you say what you want: "Just a trim, keep the length." A barber who ignores you might give you a whole new style. It might look nice, but it is not what you asked for, and it is your head. Editing works the same way. Tell the tool exactly what to change ("trim," "fix grammar") and what to keep ("my examples," "my opinion"). Then look in the mirror: reread to check it is still you.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Catch subtle changes in edited writing

questions.prompt: "Make my message more professional" added "I have extensive experience in management." The writer has none. What happened?

choices.text: Nothing; professional messages always include management experience claims
The writer gained experience
The edit added a false claim
The edit improved accuracy

questions.correct_answer: The edit added a false claim
questions.intro: Editing tools can create problems that are easy to miss. "Make it more professional" may remove warmth that mattered, or add confident claims ("I have extensive experience") that are not true. A shortened version may drop a qualifier like "usually," changing a careful statement into an absolute one. For messages that represent you, such as job applications, apologies or messages to teachers, compare the edit with your original line by line, and keep a copy of your own version.

questions.prompt: A shortened text changed "this method usually works" to "this method works." What was lost?

choices.text: The subject of the sentence
A qualifier that made the claim careful
Nothing important; "usually" is just an extra word that adds no meaning at all
The verb

questions.correct_answer: A qualifier that made the claim careful
